description: What a spectacular and challenging day.  I took a guided overnight tour that consisted of 3 parts.  A hike to a Karen Hill Tribe village in the mountains outside of Chiang Mai, an overnight stay and a return hike, then a visit to an elephant refuge and finally a float down this beautiful river on a bamboo raft.  That last one was super fun but no pics as I was worried about the phone.  This day was very challenging due to the combination of very significant heat and very steep climbs.  But we were rewarded with beautiful jungle scenery and rice paddies, an amazing waterfall, and finally the tribal village of the Karen people.  THey were very friendly and while very, very rustic the stay was a nice one.

description: We were awakened at 5am by the roosters, dogs, chickens, pigs, and all sorts of activities.  Had a simple breakfast then it was 2 hours of hiking to another waterfall and our final destination.  It was another very hot day with extrememly steep climbs and descents.  The mosquitos were there but not too hectic.  Incredible scenery all around us.  We visited an elephant 'sanctuary' which really is just a money generating business where the elephants are paraded in front of you in close proximity.  Not my favorite sort of enterprise but it was a treat to see an Asian elephant up so close.  Then we went on a river float on bamboo rafts.  Very peaceful with some gentle rapids and a very nice finish to another arduous day.  Look for photo icons to the SW of Chiang Mai if you're interested in seeing where this trek was.

O guess I should have realized but I just assumed that was like a part of it while I think it's really the main part of it.  So... description: It was a very long tour day with some really great stops.  Re-visited the White Temple which still just blows me away.  The artist who made this is just a genius.  There was a gallery of his stuff that was also incredible.  And the big bonus was a section I missed the first time called The Art Cave (or Art Garden - I think Cave...).  Just phenomenal.  This cave had so much detail with cool lighting, sculptures, music.  I found it hard to leave.  Then we hit the Blue Temple - another very cool, very modern temple not too dissimilar from the White Temple style.  Then the Black House or something like that which was an artist's (since passed) installation on this large property.  A lot of dark themes and unusual furniture and sculptures.  Another great installation.  Then to the tea farm which was pretty neato - Oolong tea tasting on a beautiful property.  Then the Tall Neck Village - which honestly was a little uncomfortable - but these people rely on this income as they are refugees from Myanmar.  You've surely seen at some point a documentary where the women of this tribe wear brass rings stacked on their necks that elongates them.  The older women still had these as did a few of the younger ones.  Felt weird taking pics so I didn't.  It was nice as there wasn't really a crowd and children were around playing their normal children games so the vibe was mostly fine.  Then the Golden Triangle which is the intersection of Thailand, Myanmar, and Laos.  Oh, and the Opium Museum which was sorta interesting - especially in that the area we spent most of the day in used to be predominantly occupied by opium fields.  Finally a quick stop at the Saturday Night Market in Chiang Rai, which I can still hear as I type this right before bed.  I have a very early morning tomorrow as I start my journey to Laos.  Should be an interesting one and it just might not be all that enjoyable.  Let's see how it goes!

description: A big travel day.  Went through Laos immigration and I have one weird story.  They want US$40 for the Visa.  I was warned they are very particular about the state of the bills themselves.  It turns out they are VERY, VERY particular.  Like no spots, crease marks, or defects of literally ANY kind.  I had 5 20's turned down and they finally took my 2nd $100 bill.  What a dump thing - they have some sort of money fetish here.  Also, $1 USD is equal to 21,340 Laotian "Kip".  Yeah.  I was told they take Thai Baht so I loaded up on that but I think that was a mistake because now I'm having to do 2 conversions just to know how much something is.  And they give you Kip for change anyhow so there's no avoiding it.  Sort of a mess but I'm sure I'll get around it.  Had a minor bad experience at the town we stopped - it's fully a we-got-you tourist trap and I some old guy hijacked my bag and insisted on payment for carrying it to shore afterwards.  Sux.  I suspect it's just this crappy town.  Hotel pretty rustic but at $13 per night what do you want?  So it's another long boat day tomorrow then hopefully things will be much better in Luang Prabang and I forked over for a pretty nice hotel there (like $35/night!!).

description: It was about a 4 hour ride by mini-van to Nong Khiaw, a fairly small village alongside the Nam Ou river in Laos.  The journey was harrowing, with a small roaded loaded with massive trucks and craters that you almost couldn't see out of.  The abuse wrought by this road on the vehicles here is just wild.  But once I made it to Nong Khiaw, I had arrived at a truly beautiful place.  My room on the river is far, far nicer than I expected and the view is just incredible.  And for the cost of about $18/night.  It started raining just as I arrived and I walked through the actually very pleasant rain to a lunch spot where the extended family was taking shelter.  Had some nice grub then took a nap back at my room.  I don't have any specific plans for this place but I might very well extend my stay for a day or two, it's so nice here.  I hear rumors of hiking and boating options so might explore those.  No temples on the menu which is a nice change of pace.

description: A nice slow day in Nong Khiaw.  Really enjoyed the very cool morning and light rain.  It was maybe 68F out at most - the nicest morning of the trip so far.  Warmed up a bit in the afternoon but still pleasant.  Got an all-day tour set up for tomorrow and also got my multi-mode transport and itinerary settled for the next leg in a few days.  All of the places I'm visiting are very tourist-oriented (it's a lot of income for them - their main income in places like Nong Khiaw), so it's quite easy to book things and arrange transport.  I was thinking the transport out of NK might be double since "they got you".  You're in this relatively remote area so good luck getting out.  But turns out it was half the price of getting here.  No way to figure this stuff out.  Pricing is kind of all over the place.  LP's purely tourist stuff was the most expensive of all the cities I've been to so far - for no particular reason that I can figure out.  That said, the most I paid for an all-day tour out of LP was $94, which isn't all that bad.  The all-day NK tour was $34, so again, no idea how these number settle out.  These all-days include lunch, water, etc. and you're grouped so it's a good time to get some social interaction in.

description: Tour day.  We got in a mini-slow boat and travelled up river for maybe 45-60 minutes and then hiked up a very rough & steep trail to a viewpoint.  Then back down to a cave used as a shelter during the US bombing of Laos - some brutal history there.  Then to a village where we hiked to a waterfall.  I told this joke in the photo caption but it's just a good joke I'll tell it again:  I was considering another tour called the 100 waterfall tour (a long hike).  I think that's about 99 waterfalls too many so opted out of that one.  Haha.  Anyhow... we then boated downriver a bit and stopped and again had to shelter from a short rain storm.  Then we jumped into some kayaks (no pics for that one so as not to risk my phone) and paddled back go our starting point under the big bridge - fun!  Stubbed my little toe at the waterfall and it's black & blue but I should be alright.  Tomorrow will be another slow day then it's off to Vang Vieng the following day.

description: Not much to show for today.  It was a markedly much hotter day in Nong Khiaw.  Prior days have been relatively pleasant while today was downright hot.  Got a coffee/banana shake mid-day to fight the heat - yeah, that's a thing here.  Really good.  Let me describe my breakfast for you:  First of all, Asian Breakfast is not something I can abide.  Hot soup and noodle for breakie not good for me.  Bigger cities accomodate Westerners well.  These smaller towns do make an attempt but...  They offer these amazing sounding banana pancakes with those really sweet and crazy good local bananas.  But there is no such thing as maple syrup in SE Asia - certainly not in the smaller towns.  They offer honey but no can do - it doesn't work.  So I skipped that and got a breakfast sandwich.  See my comments on that pic for that part of the story.  The struggle is real.

description: Travel Day to Vang Vieng, Laos.  First I had to double-back on that thing they call a road.  The minivan was so crazy packed.  They often add locals to the ride and they get a special price.  There were not enough seats for everybody so some improvisation took place and some French passengers were not pleased and let the driver know it but what can you do at that point?  A key tip I caught onto very quickly (weeks ago):  GRAB THE FRONT PASSENGER SEAT!  Get that thing as quick as you can if you think it's going to fill up.  It's THE most comfortable seat in the vehicle and has the best view of the crater-filled road you will soon be lunar crusing on.  They squeezed in a tiny local older woman between me and the driver but she was small so I was perfectly comfortable.  And no, I didn't offer my seat - she was like half my size!  OK.  So then in Luang Prabang I had to get a tuk-tuk to the train station which was like 25 minutes outside of town.  Had some terrible food but it was air-conditioned so that was nice.  The train was actually very modern and very nice and it was a very quick ride to Vang Vieng.  Had to take another shuttle to the hotel as again the train station isn't right in town.  Staying at a fairly swanky hotel and got a room upgrade (go low season!).  The plan is 4 nights here then another train ride to Vientiane for a short stay then a flight to Hanoi.

No plans for tomorrow as I'm going to see how I feel.  One thing about this place, is it's very hard to maintain being hygeienic around food.  You're constantly handling filthy money as most places don't take cards and there's not mucb in the way of soap around outside your hotel room.  And you'rr in typically pretty high population densities so like my last Thailand trip, it seemed inevitable to get me at some point.  That said, I'm not doing all that bad and hope I'll be back in business in a day or two.  Wouldn't say VV is my favorite place but it would be nice to get at least 1 or 2 activities in before I move off to the capital city of Laos, Vientiane.

description: Not a great night last night but generally feeling better throughout the day.  Train ride wasn't too bad.  Made it to Vientiane, the capitol city of Laos.  I was told by several people that it's a crap city not worth visiting and well... they were right.  I do have a full day tomorrow before my flight the next day - not sure what I'll do as my venture out tonight did not impress.  About that venture:  I had some really (relatively) expensive crap food at the rooftop restaurant.  Had a hankering for dessert but they no have dessert.  I figured, worst case I can find a market with a freezer and some ice cream.  It was dark by this point and I started down the busy, but small street of my hotel.   It was ultra sketch and just got sketchier the further I went.  Dark, quiet, industrial streets with me the only white guy in at least a few square miles.  But I was on a mission for some ice cream so I just put my head down and walked fast.  I found nothing on the roughly 2 mile walk I made.  But I did find success when I made it back to the hotel, looked across the street and spied a very tiny market that what-do-you-know had one of those ice cream freezers.  That Magnum bar was one of the better things I've had in awhile, let me tell you.  Food has not impressed lately though this is partly due to me illness and not wanting to venture very far.  Tomorrow's likely to me lame city but then I'm off to Vietname the next day where some real adventures should begin soon and I should be healthy to take them on again.

description: Travel Day.  Nothing could be in such stark contrast as taking off from the Vientiane, Laos airport (it's the capitol city of Laos) and landing in Hanoi, Vietnam.  The airport of Hanoi looks similar to what you'd see in Seoul:  a very, very modern and large international airport.  The Vientiane airport was in rough, rough shape and had 5 very rough-looking gates.  I had not previously considered the third-worldness of Laos and the (seemingly) non-third-worldness of Vietnam.  Mind you, I've only really seen the airport and my view to my apartment was heavily clouded by very strong, windy rain.  But the city - what I've seen of it - is also in stark contrast with Vientiane.  I'm sure Hanoi was quite different only 20 years ago.  Anyhow, I've heard good things about Hanoi and am happy to be here.  It will be interesting to contrast Hanoi with some of the smaller villages I'm sure to visit over the course of this next 1-1.5 months.  I should add that I hate to say I still have lingering sick that is stuck on me.  Not bad - but still in a rather weakened condition that is going to make exploring & touring difficult until I can fully shake this thing.  I haven't been this taken down by sickness - well maybe ever.  I'll probably just start with some short, nearby explorations of the city.  Which sounds great to me.  Like some Vietnamese coffe shops, etc.  And really, I need to put my Vietnam plans into better shape, including Hanoi.  I think it would be interesting to see some "war stuff" but also I think this city has much more to offer as well.

description: Got out for about 2 miles or so but then my body wore out and called it a day - yes, it sux.  But anyhow, I did a few things.  First, had some Vietnamese salt coffee (which I think is also known as egg coffee).  Both sound gross but it was quite good (some guy I met weeks ago had mentioned it to me).  Sort of a blended sweet egg frothy thing with the coffee (chilled).  Just not enough liquid - finished in about 3 gulps.  Went to the Temple of Literature which I read is more literally the Temple of Confuscious (there's a buddha-like statue of him there - people were praying to him which I found interesting).  Originally built in 1020 but rebuilt several times afterwards.  I had plans to proceed to 3 or 4 more destinations but got a little side-tracked when I looked to my left as I crossed a street and saw what appeared to be this famous alley-sized 'street' with a railroad running down the middle.  It's a tourist trap but sorta cool.  You can sit there and when the train comes by and the staff will pull the tables and chairs up and you can go "ooooh..., look at the train, it's so close".  I didn't do that myself - turns out the next train was like 4 hours later haha.  A funny piece to this story is I had been hearing this heavy rumbling intermittantly from my apartment.  Took awhile to realize it was a train - I'm in a very dense commercial area and hadn't seen any tracks so that was confusing.  It's loud but there aren't many runs so it didn't really bother me.  ANYHOW... this is the same train.  It's like right next to me.  The train.  At that point I was very thirsty and starting to feel tired so I decided to head back to my place a get some water and rest.  I took a long nap but never really recovered the mojo to get out there again.  I will head out in a bit for some food.  When I have a bigger appetite I will be trying Bun Cha which sounds incredible - look it up.  Some day my body will recover.  I just hope it's sooner than later.

description: Feeling quite a bit better today.  In fact, in 2 separate outings I walked a totatl of 7.1 miles!  That is a huge boost.  Still a few lingering things but on the whole much better!  Got 2 weeks of touring all sorted out this morning.  Headed over to Hoa Lo Prison, which was known as the "Hanoi Hilton" during the Vietnam War.  Did you know they call it the American War here?  This is also the prison that held Senator John McCain for 5-1/2 years.  I'm of course, in Vietnam so the focus of the tour/exhibits was the time that the Vietnamese revolutionaries were held here by the French and the atrocities they suffered.  The American part of the story was here but it seemed to be sorta shuffled off the main path in an upstairs area.  And the treatment of prisoners was pretty whitewashed.  Let's get real:  America's record on the treatment of "wartime" prisoners isn't so hot lately.  It was interesting to see, though only about a fifth of it is intact.  I didn't realize that Senator McCain was shot down just a few blocks from where I'm staying.  Did you know he broke both his arms and a leg in the process and he nearly died?  Go look up where he tells the whole story - it's quite interesting.  I moved on from there and basically just did some city walking, grabbed some lunch and headed back to my crib.  Not trying to overdo it as I step out of this illness.  One more full day in Hanoi tomorrow then it's off to the Ha Long Bay area for a cruise!

It's always nice to hear/share stories with co-travelers along the way.  Today:  This morning I headed over to the train street as it was only about 10 minutes away and crowds were light.  Bought a coffee as my entry fee, got a great spot and got some pics/video.  It was brief but kinda thrilling.  Headed over to the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum.  Normally his embalmed body is on public display but - and I don't know how accurate this is - the rumor has it that his body is on loan to Russia.  I dunno.  I missed seeing it - how many times do you get to see an embalmed body of a famous person?  Still, the grounds were pretty cool, very expansive, and very wet once the torrents unleashed.  Very heavy rain and lightning everywhere.  I enjoyed just hanging out and watching the lightning strikes all around me.  This site had the biggest crowds I've seen to date.  Had a very nice walk back and chilled for a bit.  Next mission: Bun Cha

description: This trip has been a real struggle at times.  Last night I developed some severe diarrhea and upset stomach.  In the morning vomiting.  Clear signs of food poisoning.  I suspect the Bun Cha but who knows.  So it was a very unpleasant day.  Started feeling worse in the afternoon and decided it was time to seek a clinic.  I was feeling so bad I just directed ChatGPT to find me a well-rated English-speaking clinic in the area.  Got a taxi there and it was a really nice, professional, modern clinic.  They took blood & stool and put me on some major fluids with an iv and also gave me anti-nausea drugs.  Was taking fluids for several hours.  They confirmed an infection and likely food-borne.  So got some antibiotics he thought were more appropriate and some anti-nausea meds.  I’ll be honest, once you have been so burned by your food it’s hard to remain confident as the impact is so harsh - as you know, it’s just such an intensely bad feeling when you get food poisoning.  So it’s hard to feel good about the next 1.5 months food-wise.  I dunno….  Fairly demotivated at the moment.  Was reading up on Vietnam and Hanoi in particular and they have had some recent isses with an increase in food poisonings.  Doesn't give me confidence for the next 2 months.

description: Updated!  Got in late last night to Sapa after a 6 hour bus ride from Ha Giang.  The prior 4 days were a group motorcycle trip with 6 other riders.  We all elected (as do 99% of tourists) to do the "easy rider" option where we have a driver.  We had to pack light as there was so support vehicle.  It's all a little sketch but I only saw one very minor spill the entire trip (that is a crazy story:  this truck left behind a large trail of oil - yes OIL - on a steep mountain downgrade.  A good samaritan was out warning bikes and cars to stop due to oil on the road.  My driver took it very easy - another one not so much and he and his rider when down - unhurt.  Some very large trucks in front of us were sliding down, barely in control.  Anyhow - we made it down ok).  We'd stop frequently - every place had a coffee shop / refereshment stand.  The universal agreement was that the coconut coffee was the best - it came in varying forms but is basically a sweet, iced coffee/coconut combo.  We'd retire at a homestay every night - do group meals and karaoke.  There was a tradition of drinking shots of "Happy Water" (very strong rice wine).  My group of 20-somethings were super fun and nice and the Aussie's put on the pressure for shot after shot so I had to not embarrass the USA so followed suit.  It was a lot of fun.  Anyhow, overall it was a series of rides, activities, eating, drinking, singing, and hanging out - a great tour with unbelievable views.

description: Got up early to hike up to the cable car station to Fansipan peak, which is the highest in Indochina (Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam) at about 10,312 ft.  You have the option to take a funicular to the station from town or do a ~40min climbing hike to the station.  I did the hike and arrived about 20min prior to the 1st tram departure, which put me ahead of the saps who had to wait for the 1st funicular to get them there.  FIRST IN LINE!  Got the 1st tram car up.  Met a family of Sapa locals and the son took a fascination with me as he really wanted to practice his English.  I told him I was from America and he said his friend also was from America - in a place called New Zealand.  It took a bit to sort that one out.  Anyhow, once we made it to the top station, I had another option to either climb the 600 steps or take another funicular for the final leg.  No way I wasn't going to take the stairs so I hauled ass up the very steep stairs, narrowly avoiding a heart attack.  Arrived at the top - FIRST!  Very quickly snapped all the photos without enjoying any of the views, just in time before the arrival of the Chinese hoard on the funicular.  Then I got to enjoy the views as I dodged all the photo-taking going on.  There was one more drama in all of this:  at the bottom station as I was waiting, I saw a guy carrying an open cardboard tray with what looked like chocolate doughnuts with sprinkles - assuming I wasn't hallucinating due to my severe craving for Western food.  These were heading for the tram cars that carried the staff and foods to the top before us passengers went up.  I made it my mission to find these at the top.  Looked everywhere - but failed to find them.  Maybe it was a hallucination.  Temperatures were in the 50's at top which was incredible considering how hot the extreme effort of the stair climbing made me.  Made it back down where the temp's were in the high 60's (Sapa is at 5K feet which really helps here) - just a dream.  Hit a cafe and then had to wait out some intense rain.  After a few beers, this total nut of a guy sat down next to me.  He was a 70-something American from Tempe who lived 3 months out of the year in Vietnam with his Hmong wife.  He asked if I wanted a tour of a market where his wife hung out and I was like, "Sure!" so he set off nearly running and I just managed to keep up.  He told me a lot of crazy stories and then showed me around where the best of the best Hmong fabrics and garments were made and sold.  I had no particular interest or luggage room so I just took it all in.  It was indeed, very beautiful stuff.  He was a funny, quirky, delightful guy and he even took me to a store and bought me some coconut candy I had asked about.  I joked as he took me upstairs in this dark stairwell that this was where he was going to kill me, right?  He didn't laugh...  At least I enjoy my own jokes.  Anyhow, I survived that one so I call it a win.

description: Late yesterday I didn't have a plan so went through the local guide website and found this hike.  They warned of its toughness but I figured I'd be just fine.  Turns out is was a BRUTAL climb.  Like straight up - there ain't no switchbacks in Vietnam.  And we started at 5K feet so the air was already getting thin.  I was told the climb was over 2K ft - felt like it.  A 62-year old village woman (looked like 78), followed us up in the hopes of a sale and she had no problem keeping up with her large bag of goods on her back.  At least the climb was first - smart.  We were in a very rural, tribal area and it was nice that it wasn't overrun by tourists - probably due to the difficulty.  You can always count on high physical input required to weed out the weak and feeble.  We had a boring lunch - except for the ice cold Coke Zero I bought.  I've never drunk these before but since the motorcycle trip, I've had quite a few.  I know it's not the absolute healthiest thing but man it tasted so good.  After lunch we hoofed it down.  At several points our guide gave us the option to take the easy route.  Thanks to my hardy Spaniard compatriots we always elected for the more scenic & difficult routes.  Saw some incredible rice fields coming down and a very cool bamboo forest.  By the end I was utterly exhausted but it was worth the price of admission.  I'm sitting on my bed just vanquished but I'll be as good as new tomorrow - which I'm planning on being a chill-out do-little day.  Before I set off to Ninh Binh which is outside of Hanoi and which starts my southward turn to the rest of Vietnam.  It's sad that I pretty much have to hit Hanoi again for the 3rd time but it's sort of the hub of the wheel for all of the northern adventures.

description: A long travel day - about 9 hours by bus from Sapa to Ninh Binh.  I'd say about 6-7 hours of that productive.  One thing you have to accept here is that vehicular transport is just... full of its own special irregularities.  This is true of Thailand and Laos as well.  For example, there's the bus to get to the bus - fine, except for the pipe smoking break the driver had to take in the middle of it as we sat there on the bus watching him.  The regular bus made all sorts of odd stops.  It's commong for them to pick up / drop off packages and many of these pick ups and drop offs are not always directly on the route.  Also, this was a point-to-point bus bus as soon as we got near to Hanoi, they started with the special drop-offs of some of the passengers where again, you're clearly straying from the direct route.  And then the capper was the bus getting washed and serviced as we sat in it.  That was a new one.  I have never had any sort of bus/van/limo transport without any of these odd irregularities.  You just have to learn to accept it as normal here.  So my new destination is just south of Hanoi:  Ninh Binh or more specifically Tam Coc which is just outside of NB.  I haven't seen too much of it but it looks like a fun little town on like a river / lake?  Since I'm now at seal level, the high temperature / humidity is back so that's going to take some getting used to again.  I was so spoiled in Sapa.  I already booked a full day tour for tomorrow - trying to beat the incoming weekend crowd of locals for a quieter tour.

description: If not actually the hottest day of the trip it was the most heat-impactful day by a large margin.  It was hot, humid, with perfectly still air and not a spot of rain.  Went on a tour and the first stop was a 500 step, very steep climb up a large rock outcrop.  I had to have still been feeling the 2 big climbs from several days ago - my legs were hurting almost immediately.  And the heat really just immediately sapped me - I probably wasn't too far from heat stroke when I forced myself to stop in some shade and drink some (luckly) cold water I had in my pack.  Was pretty out of it for the next few hours.  Just kind of a miserable day for touring.  We caught a temple, some ruins of an ancient capital city, and finally a boat ride that I was not looking forward to.  I didn't know much about it but it was clear we'd be in the sun for a 2 hour boat ride.  What I didn't know was that a good chunk of it would be in a cave system.  That turned out to be pretty incredible.  And as I say in the photo captions, it bore a striking resemblance to The Pirates of the Carribean ride - minus pirates and water slides and all that jazz.  They were packing the boats in so we followed each other in close proximity, just like the ride.  It finally started cooling off just a little so we got a little bit of relief mid-trip.  God bless the woman paddling our boat the entire 2 hours - she got a good tip at the end.  Apparently Kong: Skull Island was shot in the area but not having seen the movie, I didn't much out of that angle.  Finally made it back at about 5:30 after a very long, hot day - completely exhausted.  Tomorrow is another hot one and I will be taking it very easy.  It's supposed to cool down quite a bit after that.

description: Relax day in my air-conditioned room.  Got out once mid day and it was just brutally hot.  Tomorrow should be better.  A huge storm hit as I was out for dinner at an excellent Indian restaurant.  It is gusting with very high speeds right now and the power to my building is off.  According to the owner - as best as I could determine with his lack of English-speaking ability - was that lightning directly struck the building.  As I sat in their outdoor restaurant, I heard the loudest BOOM of thunder I think I've ever heard.  Back to the food:  I'm starting to have serious cravings of just simple foods back home - like a sandwich or burrito or whatever.  Vietnamese food not impressing me at the moment.  Maybe it will be better in the south - someone mentioned, and it makes sense, that most of the US Vietnamese food is southern in origin.  Northern Vientnamese food isn't doing it for me - but to be honest I haven't ventured out greatly, in part due to my fear of the local food due to the food poisoning bout.  Actually have mostly been eating only about 2 meals per day, which is good for my gut.  Scheduled a tour tomorrow.  Expected to be just slightly cooler with some rain

The father was really nice, and as I've done with a number of people I've sat down and lunched with, I offered my apologies for what is happening in America right now.  Anyhow.... I went back to that Indian place and feasted once more.  I figured I wasn't sick from the prior meal so I was likely safe.  Last thing:  did you hear about the boat capsizing in Halong Bay? Squat toilets - I mean, this place was really trying to draw the foreign crowd.  And no market.  There's *always* a market where you can get some chips, cookies, drinks, whatever.  So I got that burger in town later for a combo lunch-dinner - pretty good for a Vietnamese burger.  Drive was like 6 hrs - pretty standard.  The town is small - nothing special but the real draw here is the caves.  Planning on doing some cave tours tomorrow.  Oh, and exploring what an $8/night hotel is like.  It ain't bad.  No frills but not really missing anything either, other than TV and Vietnamese TV sux anyways.  And it comes with a free breakfast.

description: Today was Cave Day.  I joined a tour and visited two caves.  Paradise Cave was only discovered in 2005 and it is a massive and very long cave at 31 km, though we only hiked 1K.  We were told there's an option for a 7K hike with gear, headlamps and whatnot.  I considered but it just seems like a whole lot of hassle and I've already seen so much cave.  Btw, the largest cave in the world (Sơn Đoòng cave) is in the neighborhood but it is a massive ordeal and extremely expensive to get the chance to explore it.  So I didn't.  Sunrise Cave was most impressive - such a huge scale with massive, crazy-tall caverns.  A lot of people but manageable.  Had lunch, then we took a boat to Phong Nha Cave which is supposed to be the largest "water" cave in the world.  It too was impressive - nothing of the scale of Sunrise but still cool to view.  Another thing:  I narrowly avoided a cyclone that hit my prior desination today (I left yesterday).  What timing!  If you've made it this far, I'm going to mention a very unusual, not-so-funny thing that happened to me yesterday:  I was at a small 7-Eleven-type market full to the gills with tourists and locals.  I pass this small group of local kids and I feel this hand definitely cup my arse.  I turned around and it was obvious who did it - this, I dunno - maybe 14 year old boy who definitely had a guilty look on his face.  I lightly grabbed his arm and waggled my finger in a "NO" motion and said "Don't you ever do that!" multiple times.  He looked a little scared of me so I left it at that.  I couldn't believe it.  Not acceptable behavior for any orientation, sex, or age.  And just so f'ing weird for that to happen...

description: Today was chill day.  Spent much of the day indoors.  Arranged transport for 2 days from now and tediously looked through more local tour options.  It doesn't look good as there just isn't a good not-too-involved option that I could find.  I'll come up with something for tomorrow even if it's just walking around or maybe a bike ride or something.  But it will likely be another generally quiet day.  Then southwards off to Hue.  Had a great dinner at a local place a good walk away.  Hoping I don't get into local food trouble - at least it was really good and it's nice to finally find an excellent very local dish.  Have been looking into Vietnam War history and I'm just about to get into the thick of the combat areas, Hue being one of them.  There are hints of war things here, one of which I'd like to tour but I haven't found a good way to get there and back yet - I might still try tomorrow.  It's another cave but with a war museum sort of thing going on as this area was apparently heavily bombed by the US since it's Ho Chi Minh Trail adjacent.  One source says "During the war, the Phong Nha area was one of the North’s major staging areas for northern soldiers and supplies transiting to the front in the south. Soldiers would come from all over northern Vietnam and supplies would come from Hai Phong via a network of north-south roads in North Vietnam. Phong Nha was an entrepot; supplies would be stored in caves and then be re-loaded onto smaller vehicles, bicycles, or pedestrians for the trip south below the DMZ."

Oh, and did you hear about Thailand and Cambodia's recent clashes.  Things are getting more serious.  And the plan is to hit Cambodia in about 3-4 weeks, then back to Thailand.  So I got that going for me.

description: Today was travel day.  The bus ride wasn't too long but I was literally in a row of people on a "sleeper" bus that was 5 PEOPLE WIDE.  Think about how wide a bus is and cramming 5 people in the width of it.  2 were in the two aisles where they put these beds in.  I was at the window so I had to crawl over the guy's bed next to me to get out.  I was literally rubbing elbows with the guy next to me.  It sucked.  I am now unofficially in South Vietnam, below the old DMZ which I think is about 19 miles north of Hue, the city I'm now staying in.  This was an old capital of Vietnam and there remains a Citadel which is surrounded by fortified walls and a moat.  In 1968, the North Vietnamese Army (NVA) broke a ceasefire and initiated the Tet Offensive and one city they assaulted was Hue.  American and South Vietnamese forces spent weeks to drive them out and it was an extensive battle.  The primary Marine base in Hue used to be a few blocks from where I'm staying in the "New City" south of the Perfume River which surrounds the "Old City" or Citadel, where the NVA had mostly taken control.  It was a major battle in the war and eventually the US and South Vietnamese drove the NVA out, with significant loss of life on both sides.  Also, just west of here is another region that saw heavy US involvement in fighting (Hamburger Hill, Khe Sanh, etc.).  I am taking an all-day tour romorrow of the DMZ, Khe Sanh, some NVA tunnels, and some other places.  I find these historical tours that I can semi-relate to quite interesting.

description: Took a VERY long tour today.  Left at about 7:30am and got back at about 7pm.  It was a lot of driving since the destinations were spread out through the local region.  It was basically focused on local sites of significance from the Vietnam War.  I found the visit to the Khe Sanh airport the most interesting - you should check out a documentary on it.  A very significant battle took place there and the US Marines were surrounded by the North for several months.  It's located very high up in the hills on a plateau which seems perfect.  Except for the fact that there are some nearby even higher mountains that the North used to rain artillery down on the Americans.  I learned that tomorrow is Vietnam's primary day to honor the war dead so there were many military and other civilians out today in preface of that.  Not gonna lie, it felt just a little weird for obvious reasons.  Not many westerns at these sites honestly - primarily local tourists.  Almost no one at Khe Sanh but it's a long drive out there.  I plan to tour the Hue Citadel tomorrow so that will also be interesting since it's basically their Memorial Day.  By the way, there is an unusually large number of cemetaries scattered through the area.  A lot of shit happened here - it was a very violent number of years in this immediate region.  The Vinh Moc Tunnels visit was also super cool.  There were built by the North to shuttle supplies from inland to the coast and to protect the supplies and people from detection.  They are currently working on reinforcing the tunnels.  It's a work in progress and all the tunnels (in 3 levels) I was in had no reinforcements but the guide assured me that they have yet to have any collapses.  Oh, last thing:  I was the only person on this tour today - a first for me.  The guide is my same age and was a southerner from Saigon.  He refuses to call it Ho Chi Minh City (its official name now) and still refers to Saigon.  He said his mother was forced to cooperate with the Viet Cong when she lived there (on threat of death).  So she did and when the VC left, she was then shipped off to the city and beaten by Southern military for what she did.  It's like a no-win situation.  But she was eventually released and they moved to Hue.

description: Interesting day.  I set off on foot from the "New" city to tour the Hue Citadel, which is an old walled fortresss with many nested moats.  This is what North Vietnamese attacked and occupied as one front in the Tet Offsensive in 1968.  Once Marines got the New city under control they had a very rough and long battle in attacking the Citadel and trying to defeat the NVA there.  There is still some evidence around the city (which was largely destroyed) - bullet holes, destroyed / damaged walls, etc.  The walk around the Citadel was very, very long in severe humidity and I was exhausted by the end of it.  Stopped off at a pizza place and headed to my hotel.  Had a very peculiar incident at this moment.  Some guy on a scooter was parking, said "Hello" and I said "Hello" back.  He seemed nice and said "Where are you from?".  I said "America".  He got really excited and said "Really?"  He just seemed so excited.  He told me he worked with the US during the war (he was an older man) and that he hadn't seen any Americans since because he is now a rural farmer and just happened to be in town for a memorial.  At this point I still have my scam radar up but he seemed pretty harmless and he asked if we could share some tea and talk.  Always down for an adventure I said, "Ummm OK, sure".  So I hopped on the back of his scooter (haha) and off we went - not too far to some place that in retrospect, honestly wasn't a tea place.  And all we had was some bottled sweet peach tea.  Didn't really phase me.  We had a nice conversation.  He told me how we was an officer in the Southern army during the war and upon the fall of Saigon (he refused to call it Ho Chi Minh City), he was sent to a re-education camp for 2 years.  He talked about his family and asked me about mine.  At this point it was time to go and this is where it started to get ODD.  I got the impression that he was treating me for the conversation opportunity.  But then he said something about - I dunno - something like "can you help me?"  and something to do with buying milk (?) for his family.  He ended up buying the tea and he said there was a market nearby.  I really shoulda just opted out at that point but he had been so nice and seemed so thrilled to be talking to me.  We went off on his scooter again and ended up at this nearby small market.  He said something about "Do you want to buy the big one?"  I had no idea what he meant and I see the shop person get on a ladder and haul down this giant tin of Ensure.  I figured "fine", how much could this cost?  $5?  She announced 1 million dong which is almost $40.  I didn't have the exact conversion in my head at the time but knew it was a lot so I was like, "Uhhh no, that's too much".  So he offered "Small one?" and she pulls down a half-sized tin and it was, of course about $20.  I think I had maybe $12 in my head.  Anyhow, again, I should have just right then and there left the store but I was like "Fine" and paid for it.  He gave me a ride back to my hotel (I didn't give him the exact location at this point because my belated radar was going off).  Anyhow we parted ways and of course I realize that how nice can a guy be if he immediately is asking for financial assistance.  Whatever.  Just a bummer that I'll be very much a "No" person anytime a local comes up in the future.

So I walked around in the general area of where I'm staying which saw fierce early fighting in the Battle of Hue.  There is still plenty of evidence today of the fighting (existing structures with damage and bullet holes).  Had a nice lunch at my favorite French sandwich shop and relaxed in my room then had a nice dinner at a recommended Japanese place.  Hue's been very interesting historically.  My next stop, Hoi An should offer more scenery - though honestly the peak scenery was likely in the North and I'm now in the South so we might take a few hits in that department. description: Finally left the historically laden city of Hue.  I took the option of a bus/tour combo which was actually decent.  OK, there was only one good stop of the four, but it was a really good one (Marble Mountain in Da Nang).  In Hoi An now, which is a very old trading city with heavy Chinese and Japanese influences from those trading days.  The old town was really hopping.  Too much so actually - there were untold number of humanity milling about.  But there were so many shops, restaurants it didn't really feel crowded.  Ok it felt REALLY crowded.  But it was still a good vibe and it was fun to be in such a hip town/city with so many interesting food options.  I went Mexican and I don't regret it - I didn't expect much but it was fabulous.  It doesn't seem like a city where I'd go on a tour.  Rather just self-exploration.  There is supposed to be a nice beach area to the north but at the same time it's in the 90's now so I dunno.

description: Mostly a quiet day.  The tours available aren't really my cup of tea so opting to just hang and at least get out into the Old Town at night which is quite the scene.  I'm tempted to do a wood-carving demo / class that comes highly recommended.  Maybe.  Saw a very cool show in the vein of Cirque du Soleil tonight.  Front row seats!  Paid a fair amount (for Vietnam) but I think it was worth it.  THe acrobatics and staging were excellent and the music was fantastic with so many unusual cultural instruments of Vietnam.  And the costumes and theme was very much Vietnam culture so that was nice.  I really enjoyed it.  Sometimes I come from things like this more enthralled and inspired by the music.  The just radical instruments and tones, etc really speak my language.  I'm due for a haircut so that is on the agenda tomorrow - should be an experience.

description: Another fairy quiet day.  I think that's really what Hoi An is about.  It's not about sights and tours, it's about experiencing and hanging out in the town.  Not doing much day stuff either as we're solidly in the 90's right now.  But I did manage to get out and get a much needed haircut.  This place was great and they added a hair wash and head rub too.  These come after the haircut where I recall in the US you'd get a wash before??  I dunno, I only do a barber these days at home.  He did a great job and it was less than $8, which I suspect is expensive for here.  Had a nice night walk through town and had a light dinner as well. I signed up for a wood carving class for tomorrow that should be fun.

I have 2 bones to pick with the T/T Bar (one for each T).  "Unique Egg Beer - Must Try".  It's unique for a reason:  no one in their right mind would mix those two things.  And what dumbshit passed up calling the Egg Espresoo Martini an "EGGspresso Martini"?  It's like they're not even trying.
I got a haircut today.  It was fun.  Boats in focus tho which I think is the right choice.

Dinner haha.  I had 2 of these amazing orange juices and I was like SOOOOO thirsty at that point.  It's difficult to stay hydrated here as you just sweat ALL the time.  Added a banana smoothie and some weird peanut cake things I bought off a lady on the street.
Selfie with banana smoothie. I think this was an accidental pic because I don't remember taking it.

I pass this open area every night on the way to Old Town.  There's always something going on - martial arts, what have you.  Tonight it was drum class and it was fun to watch - I would LOVE to play in a drum troop like this.

description: Another relatively quiet day.  In the morning went a little outside of Hoi An to a place that makes exquisite wood carvings.  Took a ~3 hour class where we made our own carving.  I did Baby Yoda.  It took a lot of patience - more than I think I have to take this on as a hobby.  But it was a lot of fun and the instructors were very helpful.  Temperatures and humidity pretty brutal right now but we have be3n saved by some fair winds.  This kind of temp/humidity without wind makes it so, so much worse.  I suspect that having left the cooler, rainier regions, this is likely the norm until the end of the trip.  We'll see.  I'm heading back to Da Nang for several days staying in a high-rise just off the beach.  Then it's to Ho Chi Minh City AKA Saigon.

description: Very short trip to Da Nang.  This is a change of pace as I'm living large in a beach-front hotel, though still only about $60/night which is far from the sub $20 I've been managing for most of the past month.  But I wanted to have a nice just relax near the beach stay with a nice beach view from the 17th floor.  Not that I'll be doing much going to the beach given the almost 100 degree temps with high humidity.  It's brutal out there.  But it's nice to have a relaxing stay in a nice place.  You be surprised, there are still a few luxury resorts in the area in the $1000+ range and quite a few in the $300-plus range.  One thing I've discovered is that at least when traveling on my own, I don't need the fancy places - though they are nice once in awhile.  In Saigon, all of the top TripAdvisor spots were $100+ but I ended up taking a $14/night place that has a private room & bath and seems perfectly fine for my needs.  Getting close to wrapping up Vietnam - it's hard to believe! I've got my visa to Cambodia and just need to finalize my Saigon plans so I can book my flight.

description: Took a full day tour with a fun group.  A LOT of driving - about 6 of the 12 hours was driving.  This is kind of the main tour in the area - at least the Cu Chi Tunnels part so it was very crammed with people but they had it set up pretty well to handle the numbers.  These tunnels are near the Cambodia border outside of Saigon and represent the end of the line of the Ho Chi Minh Trail / Supply Line.  As you might imagine the area was bombed a lot by the US and thus they had these crazy network of tunnels (remember Forest Gump?).  We saw just a few of them.  The tour guide was a nice guy but man did he rip the US a new arsehole.  Probably deserved over what happened but yeah, being the only American in a van full of other nationalities was fun while he ranted on and on.  I was willing to take the heat for that.  Some clear misrepresentations and of course Kennedy was killed by the CIA, etc., etc.  Anyhow - it was an interesting tour.  The 2nd half of the tour we drove to the Mekong Delta which is a vast region in the area of the Mekong River which is just massive at this point in its journey to the sea.  It was sort of an odd collection of stops on 2 different islands in the delta.  Every stop was selling something but they were still interesting just the same.  A lot of tip pressure for - I dunno - like 10 different people along the way.  Unlike all the other tours I've been on in that there was really no tip pressure at all.  Whatever - the tour wasn't as expensive as some of those others so I didn't mind too much.  Weather, while still very humid, was mostly forgiving today and we escaped any real heavy-duty heat.
